battle.title: Interview Warm-Up
battle.description: Ask the right questions before you write a single line of code.

questions.text: The interviewer says: "Find the duplicates in an array." What do you do FIRST?
options: Start coding a nested loop right away, since it is the simplest approach
Ask clarifying questions: element types, size, return all duplicates or one, may I modify input
Say you will use a HashMap and begin writing it
Ask the interviewer to give you the optimal solution so you can learn from it
questions.answer: Ask clarifying questions: element types, size, return all duplicates or one, may I modify input
questions.explanation: The statement is deliberately vague, and the answers change the design (sorting in place, a set, or a bit trick). Jumping straight to code, even with a good data structure, risks solving the wrong problem.

questions.text: What is the main purpose of clarifying questions at the start of a coding interview?
options: To buy thinking time so the interviewer thinks you are slow to answer
To show the interviewer that you already know the answer
To make the interviewer simplify the problem until it is trivial
To pin down inputs, outputs, constraints and edge cases so you solve the real problem
questions.answer: To pin down inputs, outputs, constraints and edge cases so you solve the real problem
questions.explanation: Clarifying is about scope and correctness, not stalling or showing off. Interviewers watch whether you gather requirements the way you would on a real team.

questions.text: You asked about input size and the interviewer did not answer, saying only "you decide". What is the strongest move?
options: State an assumption out loud (say up to 10^5 elements) and offer to revisit it
Silently assume a tiny input so any solution works
Refuse to continue until the interviewer gives exact numbers
Assume the worst case is impossible and ignore constraints altogether
questions.answer: State an assumption out loud (say up to 10^5 elements) and offer to revisit it
questions.explanation: Stating assumptions makes your reasoning visible and lets the interviewer correct you early. Silent assumptions are the classic failure, and refusing to proceed looks inflexible.

questions.text: Which set of questions best targets edge cases for "reverse a string"?
options: Which language, which IDE, and can I use Google
How many test cases will you run and how long do I have
Can it be empty or null, is it unicode, and do I reverse in place or return a new string
Is this question from a real company and does it have a known answer
questions.answer: Can it be empty or null, is it unicode, and do I reverse in place or return a new string
questions.explanation: Good clarifying questions probe the data and the contract: empty or null input, character set, and in-place versus new output. Questions about tooling or the question's origin say nothing about correctness.

questions.text: After clarifying, what is the best next step before coding?
options: Say nothing and code for ten minutes so you do not waste time
Restate the problem and assumptions, walk through a small example, and confirm
Ask the interviewer if your future solution will be accepted
Immediately state the final time complexity before describing any approach
questions.answer: Restate the problem and assumptions, walk through a small example, and confirm
questions.explanation: Restating with a small example confirms shared understanding and catches mistakes while they are cheap. Silent coding hides your thinking, and quoting complexity before choosing an approach is premature.
